items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: ‘Cause you called Nat Hentoff and you said, ‘I got all this Joe Williams stuff,” and Nat said, “Call Joel.” You and I spoke the next thing we know we have “Havin’ a Good Time” with Joe Williams.

ctx.x: Yeah, that’s not what I mean.

Yeah. No. I got a stash of tapes that no one’s ever heard. I have a way that I do compilations. I have this little area, I started playing it because when I came back after that slump in the early eighties I had to come up with something new. Because the pop records I was making and the jazz records I was making, nobody really wanted. So, this © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

is too long a story to bore you with but through a friend, Bernie Dreighton, I found some tapes he had made at a small club in Brooklyn in the sixties: Blakey, Kenny Dorham, you know, people like that, guys who’d play these small clubs in Brooklyn to work out material before they recorded for Blue Note or Prestige or stuff like that. So in trying to clear those, I came across other collections. At a certain point we had isolated a quarter of a million hours of privately — in lieu of the word illegally — recorded…

items.q: there’s a man named Joel Dorn who recently put out a superb collection of the major gospel recordings.

ctx.x: At that point in Boston, did you get to experience the black church or the black dances in person? When did that happen?

No, I didn’t get to the black churches until I came to New York. Then I was in Harlem one day and I walked into – I didn’t even know what it was, but there were trombones, people were playing tambourines, and the preachers and the singing. It was Daddy Grace. I went to some of those afterwards as well. I wish I still had those recordings. In fact there are some – there’s a man named Joel Dorn who recently put out a superb collection of the major gospel recordings. Talk about music as joy.
Can you remember the names of any of the preachers whose recordings you had?
